Gibeah of Saul
GIB-ee-uh of SAWL
proper noun
From the Hebrew gibeah, meaning “hill”; called “of Saul” because it was the home and capital of Israel’s first king.

See also: Gibeah of Saul

Biblical Definition

Gibeah of Saul, also called Gibeah of Benjamin, was a town in the territory of Benjamin that became famous twice over — once for shame and once for honor. In the dark days of the Judges, when there was no king in Israel and every man did that which was right in his own eyes, the men of Gibeah committed the abominable outrage against the Levite’s concubine, a wickedness so vile that it provoked civil war and nearly blotted out the whole tribe of Benjamin (Jdg 19–20). The horror of Gibeah became a byword for depravity, recalled long after by the prophets (Hos 9:9; Hos 10:9). Yet from this same Benjamite town came Saul the son of Kish, whom God gave as Israel’s first king. After his anointing, “Saul also went home to Gibeah; and there went with him a band of men, whose hearts God had touched” (1Sa 10:26). Gibeah became his royal seat, the place to which the tidings of Jabesh-gilead came (1Sa 11:4), and the hill where he held his court under the tree (1Sa 22:6). The town thus stands as a double witness: of the depths to which men sink when each is his own law, and of the LORD’s patient ordering of His people’s history, raising a king even from a tribe that had once nearly destroyed itself by its own sin.

Webster 1828 Definition

A town of Benjamin, home and capital of King Saul, also the scene of the Levite’s concubine outrage in the days of the Judges.

expand to see more

GIBEAH OF SAUL, a town of Benjamin, the home and royal seat of Saul the son of Kish.

It was the scene of the Levite’s concubine outrage that sparked civil war (Jdg 19–20).

Saul returned to it after his anointing, with men whose hearts God had touched (1Sa 10:26).

Tidings of Jabesh-gilead came to it, moving Saul to deliver them (1Sa 11:4).

The prophets recalled its sin as a byword of Israel’s corruption (Hos 10:9).

Key Scripture

1Sa 10:26 — "And Saul also went home to Gibeah; and there went with him a band of men, whose hearts God had touched."

1Sa 11:4 — "Then came the messengers to Gibeah of Saul, and told the tidings in the ears of the people: and all the people lifted up their voices, and wept."

Jdg 20:5 — "And the men of Gibeah rose against me, and beset the house round about upon me by night, and thought to have slain me: and my concubine have they forced, that she is dead."

Hos 10:9 — "O Israel, thou hast sinned from the days of Gibeah: there they stood: the battle in Gibeah against the children of iniquity did not overtake them."

Modern Corruption

The lesson to recover is that where each man is his own law, abomination follows; yet God still orders His people’s history in mercy.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Gibeah is the bitter fruit of moral autonomy. “Every man did that which was right in his own eyes,” and Gibeah is the result — an outrage so foul it tore the nation apart. The age that despises objective law and exalts the self as the only standard is an age that breeds new Gibeahs.

Yet the same town gives a second word. From sin-stained Benjamin God raised Saul to be king, showing that He works His purposes even through unworthy material. The believer learns to dread the depravity of the human heart left to itself, and to marvel at the patient providence of God, who governs the unfolding of redemption through flawed men and shameful places.

Hebrew Roots

The name simply means “hill”; the addition “of Saul” distinguishes it as the seat of Israel’s first king.

expand to see more

Gibeah — from the Hebrew for “hill” or “height.”

It is kin to Geba and Gibeon, all from the same hill-root.

“Of Saul” marks it as the king’s town, distinct from other hills.

It is also styled Gibeah of Benjamin after its tribe.

Such height-names abounded in the rugged ridge country of Benjamin.

Usage

"Saul ruled from Gibeah, the hill town of his fathers."

"The sin of Gibeah became a byword for Israel’s corruption."

"Messengers brought word to Gibeah of Saul, and the people wept."
